data.title: Anthropic vs. the Pentagon: What It Means for Claude Code
data.excerpt: What happened between Anthropic and the US government in 2026, from the federal directive to the court rulings, and what it means if you use Claude Code.

children.text: Updated November 3, 2026. An earlier version of this article described an executive order that named Claude Code. We could not verify that such an order exists, so we rewrote it around what the public record shows: a presidential directive, two Pentagon "supply chain risk" designations and several court rulings. Every fact below links to its source.

If you write code with Claude Code, you may have read that the US government "banned" it. The real story is narrower and still moving through the courts. This guide lays out the timeline and what it means in practice depending on who you are: a private company, a Department of War contractor or a federal agency.
The short answer
Private companies and freelancers:
Anthropic has said that individual customers and commercial access are unaffected. The legal fight is about government use.
Department of War contractors:

an appeals court upheld, in September 2026, the Pentagon's power to bar Anthropic products from work on its contracts. Wait for written direction from your contracting officer and keep that work separate.
Federal civilian agencies:
a federal judge blocked the presidential directive in March 2026, and in October 2026 Anthropic announced a General Services Administration (GSA) agreement through which agencies can buy Claude.
February 2026: the directive and the designation

The dispute started over contract terms. Anthropic wanted guarantees that its models would not be used for mass domestic surveillance of Americans or for fully autonomous weapons; the Pentagon said it needed to use them for "all lawful purposes" (
Defense One, February 27, 2026
On
February 27, 2026

, President Trump posted on Truth Social that he was directing every federal agency to immediately stop using Anthropic's technology, with a six-month phase-out for agencies already using its products (
NBC News

). The same day, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said he was directing the Department of War to designate Anthropic a supply chain risk to national security, and wrote that no contractor, supplier or partner that does business with the US military may conduct any commercial activity with Anthropic (
CBS News

Anthropic answered that a designation under 10 U.S.C. 3252 "can only extend to the use of Claude as part of Department of War contracts," that access for individual customers and commercial contracts was unaffected, and that it would challenge the designation in court (
Anthropic, February 27, 2026

). On March 4 it received a letter confirming the designation; in a statement the next day it said the designation applies only to the use of Claude "as a direct part of" contracts with the Department of War, and that "the vast majority" of its customers are unaffected (
Anthropic, March 5, 2026
The court rulings
There are two separate designations and two separate cases.
California: the directive and the first designation are blocked

US District Judge Rita Lin, in San Francisco, granted Anthropic a preliminary injunction. It blocked agencies from carrying out the ban and halted the Pentagon's actions to enforce the supply chain risk designation. Lin wrote that "punishing Anthropic for bringing public scrutiny to the government's contracting position" is "classic illegal First Amendment retaliation" (
FedScoop, March 27, 2026
August 27, 2026:
Lin ruled on the merits that the Pentagon acted illegally by punishing Anthropic for its criticism (
AP via NPR, August 28, 2026
). According to an analysis by the law firm Taft, the decision set aside the designation made under 10 U.S.C. 3252, which remains subject to a permanent injunction (
Taft
Washington, D.C.: the second designation is upheld
September 25, 2026:

in a separate case over a different law, the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act (FASCSA, 41 U.S.C. 4713), the D.C. Circuit ruled 2-1 for the Pentagon. Judges Gregory Katsas and Neomi Rao formed the majority; Judge Karen LeCraft Henderson dissented. The ruling lets the Pentagon keep removing Claude from its systems and bar the use of Anthropic products for Department of War work, but Anthropic's products are not barred from the federal government as a whole. Anthropic said it "respectfully disagrees" and is considering further review (
AP, September 25, 2026
What it means if you use Claude Code
At a private company or as a freelancer

Claude Code is an Anthropic product, so it falls under the same statements: Anthropic says commercial access is unaffected, and none of the rulings above restricts private use outside government contracts. You don't need to change anything. If your company also sells to the government, read the next section.
As a Department of War contractor

After the D.C. Circuit ruling, the Department of War can use FASCSA to direct contractors to stop using Anthropic products in the performance of its contracts. Taft's guidance is to wait for written direction from a contracting officer through a contract modification, to monitor SAM.gov for supply chain security orders, and to keep "a strict separation from any DoW work" if you keep using Anthropic products commercially (
Taft
). In practice, that starts with knowing where Claude Code touches code or documents you deliver to the Department of War, so you can separate it when asked. Our guide to
governing AI agents in a company
covers how to keep that kind of inventory.
At a federal civilian agency

On October 27, 2026, Anthropic announced an expanded GSA agreement with a 40% discount on Claude Enterprise, Claude for Government and the Claude API, and said agencies "can buy Claude" through GSA's Multiple Award Schedule (
Anthropic, October 27, 2026
). Procurement rules can still change with further appeals, so check with your contracting office before relying on it.
What is still open

Anthropic said after the September ruling that it is considering all options, including further review, and AP reported in August that the government was expected to contest the California decision. We'll update this article if a court changes the picture. Separately, for commercial users, in May 2026 Anthropic
signed a compute deal with SpaceX and doubled Claude Code's five-hour limits

children.text: Was Claude Code banned by an executive order?

We found no executive order that singles out Claude Code. On February 27, 2026, President Trump posted a directive telling federal agencies to stop using Anthropic's technology, with a six-month phase-out, and the Pentagon moved to label Anthropic a supply chain risk. A federal judge blocked the directive and that designation in March 2026.
Can private companies keep using Claude Code?

Anthropic has said that individual customers and commercial access are unaffected. The dispute is about government use, and the restriction upheld by an appeals court in September 2026 covers the use of Anthropic products in Department of War contract work.
What should a Department of War contractor do?

Follow the written direction of your contracting officer and watch for supply chain security orders. Law firm guidance after the September 2026 ruling recommends keeping any use of Anthropic tools strictly separate from Department of War contract work.
